exercise_name: Turn Problems Into Punchlines — full pipeline
description: Carter's master move and the headline of the workbook's Section 1 (48 exercises). Start from a personal problem, attach an attitude (weird/scary/hard/stupid), rant the 'because...', sharpen it into a specific truthful premise, then find an act-out and a mix. Reframes 'be funny' (paralysing) as 'what's bugging you?' Comedy as self-healing: feel the pain, then laugh in its face.

exercise_name: Topic mining from pain — list what's wrong
description: Generate raw material by listing the things that trouble you: what you hate, what annoys you, what you worry about, what you're afraid of, and what you're ashamed of. These problems are the fuel for jokes, since Carter holds that stand-up is the art of turning your own problems into punchlines.

Take a topic and label it with one of the four basic comic attitudes: weird, scary, hard, or stupid. Say '(topic) is weird/scary/hard/stupid.' Carter's core reframe: thinking in terms of what is weird/stupid/scary/hard, rather than what is funny, frees the creative process and points you at the joke.

Speak (don't write) about why your topic is weird/scary/hard/stupid: '(topic) is hard because...' and rant out loud, walking around. Interrogate it with 'Why is it weird? Why is it stupid? Why is it hard? Why is it scary?' The rant surfaces premises conversationally instead of forcing jokes on the page.

Turn a ranted angle into a premise: a cut-to-the-chase, get-to-the-point, original observation that is truthful and relatable, about 1-2 lines. Not a description of what happened. 'Get specific - funny is in the details.' The premise is the serious, factual setup the punch will pay off.

exercise_name: Act-out — perform it, don't tell it
description: Instead of describing a person or thing in your setup, become it and play the moment as a scene. Turn into the people/things you mention and literally act them out (long or short). Carter: 'the laughs are in the execution of the act-outs.' This is the highest-value funny move in her formula.

exercise_name: Acting-Out Premises (with reveal at the end)
description: Given a plain premise, invent an act-out that plays it as a scene; for several prompts, withhold the key context (the person's age, the location, who is speaking) and 'reveal at the end' so the reveal is the punch. Practice set in the free workbook uses premises about body piercing, airports, a co-dependent dog, etc.

Add an angle by mixing: either compare any two things, or change the environment. Comparison templates include Before vs Now, Them vs Me, and Men vs Women. Environment-swap: take your subject and drop them into a different occupation/setting (e.g. put your self-absorbed mother on a suicide hotline) to expose the funny.

exercise_name: Comparison Jokes — Before vs Now / Them vs Me / Men vs Women
description: A fill-in mix drill: write comparison jokes across three frames. Before vs Now (how your standards/hopes dropped over time), Them vs Me (celebrities/others vs your reality), and Men vs Women (contrasting how each handles the same thing). Each frame sets up a clean two-sided contrast for the punch.

Build a list joke where the third item is the funny one. Practice with explicit rhythm patterns specified per prompt: big/big/small, small/small/big, obvious/obvious/weird, subtle/subtle/obvious. Worksheet prompts include 'It's a scary world: terrorism, war, ___' and '3 signs your relationship is over.'

A 3-beat self-deprecation formula with delivery dynamics: make a big BOLD boastful 'lie' (loud) -> Admission One (quieter, partly walk it back) -> Admission Two (soft, embarrassed, the pathetic real truth) -> snap back to 'Anyway!' (loud). Example: 'I lost 120 pounds!' ... 'well, not all at once' ... 'I just lost and gained the same 10 pounds twelve times. Anyway!'

Fill-in identity joke: 'You may not know this, but I'm half ___ and half ___, and that means I ___.' First list your ethnicity, parents' nationalities, hobbies, and current/past jobs, then combine two of them so the clash produces the punch (e.g. 'half jock and half nerd... I beat myself up after school').

Fill-in fake-etymology joke: 'You may not know this, but [industry term] is actually a [language] term, meaning [your real frustration].' First list the jargon of your job and what frustrates you about it, then fuse them (e.g. 'entrepreneur is French for I work in my underwear'; 'PowerPoint is Sanskrit for boring-ass presentation').

Take a real acronym from your job and re-spell it so each letter expresses your frustrations. List your work acronyms and your job's frustrations/hazards/inconveniences, then map the letters onto the gripes (e.g. FORD = Found On Road Dead; IOWA = Idiots Out Wandering Around).

Self-deprecation seed list: write down at least three things people joke about you behind your back, then circle the most embarrassing one. The most embarrassing truth becomes your strongest, most authentic material - 'authenticity is the secret sauce.'

After a joke lands, pile on more punchlines off the same setup without writing a new setup. Tags are how you wring multiple laughs from one premise; they feed the three-laughs rule (below). Keep tagging until the premise is exhausted.

Quality filter: if a joke can't earn at least three laughs in its telling (often via tags), rework it or throw it out. Apply it during 'Throwing Out the Clunkers' to prune a set down to only material that pulls its weight.

Group all your jokes that share a topic into a continuous 'run,' so the act flows by subject rather than as disconnected one-liners. A named step in the 'Days to Killer Comedy Material' arc; it also helps you find gaps where you need more material on a topic.

Reference an earlier punchline/topic later in the set so the audience gets a bonus laugh from the recognition. A standard polish move Carter teaches alongside tags and topic runs for tightening a set.

Order your polished jokes into a running set, organized by time and theme (Section 4 of the workbook = a place to store set lists). The 'Getting It Funny 3-Day Jam Session' walks through organizing the set list, honing it, and a dress rehearsal before performing.

Section 5 of the workbook: 30 daily writing prompts to generate fresh raw material. Embodies the 'write every day' commandment ('your funny bone is a muscle - use it or lose it') and the 'numbers game' belief that more pages = more chances at truly inventive material.

An 'Advanced Stand-up Exercises' set of daily practices to keep generating material from real life - notice the funny as it happens, capture it, and bounce ideas conversationally rather than writing alone. Reinforces the every-day-writing habit (Carter's Seinfeld-style discipline).

Pair up with a 'comedy buddy' (someone you're comfortable with, who shows up, and thinks you're funny) and work the book's exercises together. Carter prescribes this to beat fear, procrastination and creative anxiety, since 'very few comics create material alone' and being conversational about a topic generates organic material.
A day in the arc: mine the news/current events for topics, then run them through the attitude + premise + act-out pipeline to keep your act timely and 'cutting-edge.'

A study exercise early in the program: watch comics perform and analyze their joke structure (setup/premise/act-out) to internalize the mechanics before/while writing your own. Comedy Career in a Box does the same by dissecting jokes from 36 working comics.

exercise_name: Performance Review — rework after a set
description: After performing, review what landed and what died ('How Good Were You?'), then rework/hone the material ('Honing Material - Take Two') and prep for a second performance. Iterate via real audience feedback rather than guessing on the page.

Aim your jokes at the rich and powerful, never down at vulnerable or marginalized groups (Commandment: 'Thou Shalt Bash the Powerful'). A targeting rule for choosing whom a premise attacks, keeping the act both ethical and crowd-friendly.

exercise_name: Find your authentic persona / 'the message of you'
description: Build a comic voice and point of view from your real self, vulnerabilities and lived truth rather than a put-on character - 'authenticity is the secret sauce of your act.' Carrying through to her speaking work (The Message of You), the comic persona is your true self amplified.

A book track ('Creating Your Own One-Person Show'): weave your topic runs and most authentic 'pain into punchlines' material into a longer autobiographical solo show with a through-line (Carter's own model: her play A Death-Defying Escape!).

exercise_name: Section 1 — 48 Exercises to Turn Problems into Punchlines (full drill bank)
description: The workbook's headline Section 1 is a bank of 48 named exercises that each take a personal problem and convert it to a punchline. The named formula drills captured separately in this file (Reluctant Admission, Half-and-Half Mashup, Re-defining Frustrations, Acronyms, List of 3, Acting-Out Premises, Comparison Jokes, Making Fun of Yourself) are a confirmed subset; the remaining individual exercises are paywalled inside the workbook and their specific names/contents are not public (marked inferred, not fabricated).
